claims.text: The starting alloy is a rapidly solidified, metastable Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The starting microstructure consists primarily of a solid-solution matrix with dispersed minority intermetallic phases.
Mg is initially distributed homogeneously in the metastable solid solution.
Moderate-temperature annealing triggers microstructural evolution in the alloy.
Annealing promotes diffusion-driven Mg segregation to grain boundaries.
Annealing causes Mg-rich intermetallic compounds to precipitate.
Mg-rich grain-boundary phases facilitate formation of a stable protective oxide layer at high temperature.
Formation of the protective oxide layer improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Mg-rich precipitates create compositional inhomogeneity and local galvanic couples within the alloy.
The local galvanic couples increase susceptibility to aqueous corrosion.
The annealed alloy will have a higher aqueous corrosion rate than the as-solidified metastable alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies to alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³.
The proposed mechanism applies to rapidly solidified alloys containing non-equilibrium phases before annealing.
Annealing atmosphere, inert versus oxidizing, is expected to permit comparison of intrinsic microstructural evolution and oxidation-associated evolution.
The hypothesis is falsified if annealing produces no statistically significant Mg grain-boundary segregation or Mg-rich intermetallic formation.
The hypothesis is falsified if annealing fails to improve oxidation resistance or fails to increase aqueous-corrosion vulnerability relative to the as-solidified baseline.
